tier_justification: Folklore non-invertibility of greedy maximal frame cancellation in separation logics with disjointness conflict (consistent with Charguéraud 2020 Appendix K, which notes generically, without naming specific rules, that some `xsimpl` simplifications are not equivalence-preserving), made precise with illustrative (not minimal) linear (`CellModel`) and affine (`TwoCellModel`) finite countermodels plus a witness separating partial from maximal cancellation; two-element models (`Toy.SepAC.boolOr_linear_cancelAtoms_converse_fails`, `Toy.SepAC.boolAnd_affine_cancelAtoms_converse_fails`) and `CellModel` under `affineCellEntails` (`Toy.SepAC.cellModel_affine_cancelAtoms_converse_fails`) also exhibit the failure.
plain_claim: Even when all ACU, preorder, and monotonicity laws hold, maximal syntactic cancellation (`cancelAtoms`) is not invertible: (1) in the linear 1-cell conflict model `CellModel` (`¬ AffineEntails`), `(owned ∗ owned) ⊢ owned` holds while `cancelAtoms` yields the false residual `owned ⊢ empty` (a residual that becomes valid under affine `affineCellEntails`); (2) in the affine 2-cell conflict model `TwoCellModel` (`AffineEntails`), `(cellA ∗ cellA) ⊢ (cellA ∗ cellB)` holds while `cancelAtoms` yields the false non-`emp` residual `cellA ⊢ cellB`; and (3) on `((0 ∗ 0) ∗ 0) ⊢ (0 ∗ 0)` in `CellModel`, maximal `cancelAtoms` fails whereas partial cancellation (`common = [0]`) leaves the valid residual `conflict ⊢ owned`.
non_claims: `CellModel.entails` is linear (`owned ⊬ empty`). In affine logics, where every assertion entails `emp`, the exhibited residual `owned ⊢ empty` is valid (`Toy.SepAC.affineCellEntails_residual_holds`), so the single-cell linear witness does not by itself show incompleteness for affine logics. An affine witness needs a residual whose right-hand side is not `emp` (provided by `Toy.SepAC.twoCellModel_affine_cancelAtoms_converse_fails`, and also by `Toy.SepAC.cellModel_affine_cancelAtoms_converse_fails` and `Toy.SepAC.boolAnd_affine_cancelAtoms_converse_fails`).

Refutes completeness/invertibility of maximal syntactic cancellation (`cancelAtoms`), NOT soundness (`Toy.SepAC.acu_entails_of_common_perm_of_sepMonoRight`): a non-maximal common sub-multiset cancellation can still succeed where `cancelAtoms` fails (`Toy.SepAC.partial_cancellation_succeeds_where_cancelAtoms_fails`).

plain_claim: For all trees `l, r : Tree`, the accumulator-plus-merge-sort boolean check `checkPermSort l r` equals `l.atoms.isPerm r.atoms`, `atomsFast` equals `atoms` without `List.append`, and `atomsFast.length = atomCount ≤ size`.

non_claims: Asymptotic time complexity is informal, not formalized in a machine cost model: `atomsFast` visits each `Tree` constructor once ($O(|t|)$, vs $O(|t|^2)$ worst-case for `Tree.atoms` on left-nested spines) and `List.mergeSort (· ≤ ·)` performs $O(m \log m)$ `Nat` comparisons where $m = \text{atomCount} \le \text{size}$ (vs $O(m^2)$ comparisons for core Lean's `List.isPerm`).
Each `Nat` comparison in Lean's kernel takes time proportional to the bit-length of the index ($O(\log k)$ for `Nat` literals), though reification assigns dense indices $0, \dots, m - 1$.

Critical Lean `v4.34.1` kernel caveat: core Lean defines `List.mergeSort` (`Init.Data.List.Sort.Basic`, lines 79-87) by well-founded recursion (`termination_by xs => xs.length`), replaced at runtime via the `@[csimp]` theorem `List.mergeSort_eq_mergeSortTR₂` (`Init.Data.List.Sort.Impl`, line 240). The logical definition uses well-founded recursion, and on the instances probed by `support/KernelReductionProbe.lean` the Lean `v4.34.1` kernel neither reduces `checkPermSort l r` to `true` by `whnf` nor accepts `checkPermSort l r ≡ true`, so `Eq.refl true` does not prove `checkPermSort l r = true` there, whereas the probed structurally recursive `List.isPerm` instance reduces (execution observation; not proved for all `l, r`). A reflective kernel closing its side condition via `mkEqRefl` should therefore keep structural `List.isPerm`, use a structurally recursive sort, or rewrite with `Toy.SepAC.checkPermSort_eq_isPerm_and_size_bounds` first.
Core Lean's own reflective AC tactic sorts with a structurally recursive insertion sort (`Lean.Data.AC.sort`). It is quadratic but kernel-reducible, which is consistent with the caveat above.
